sections.text:
Mordecai walks into the middle of the city in sackcloth and ashes, wailing loudly and bitterly. A decree has gone out to destroy all the Jews. Word reaches Esther in the palace, and she is the queen, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai. She cannot simply walk in and ask the king for help: whoever comes to him uninvited faces death, unless he holds out the golden scepter.

Mordecai sends back a question that has been remembered ever since: “for such a time as this”. Esther answers with fasting, and with courage: “if I perish, I perish.”

The official Haman had obtained the decree. Now the plot is reversed. Haman falls, the Jews are allowed to defend themselves, and the feast of Purim is founded to remember the rescue.

The king, Ahasuerus, is usually identified with Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 before Christ. In the Hebrew text God is never named. The ancient Greek version includes extra passages with prayers, which are part of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

Many read the silence about God as the point of the book: his care is at work in what looks like coincidence. Jews read Esther aloud every year at Purim. How the book relates to Persian history is debated among scholars. Christians read it as a story of God preserving his people when they are powerless, and of courage used for others.
